title: How can we make our own number system?
description: A number system is built from a stroke for each object, with a circle for every group of five strokes and a square for every group of five circles. The video tests it on the two questions from the book: does it ever end, and is it convenient to count with.
teaching_notes: One idea: any fixed-order sequence is a number system if it never runs out and is convenient to count with. The example here is only one choice, so accept any system that passes both tests. Watch for systems that stop at a fixed last symbol.

source: Figure it Out (the mechanism of counting, question 3)
video_script.why: The child builds a number system and tests it with the two questions used to compare sticks, letters and Roman symbols.
video_script.substitution: Pick marks, say what each mark stands for, then test the system for ending and for convenience.
video_script.anchor: a row of strokes, with a circle standing for five strokes and a square standing for five circles
video_script.payoff_line: A fixed order that never runs out and is convenient makes a number system

final_answer.value: Open answer: any fixed-order sequence that never runs out and is convenient to count with; for example, a circle for every group of five strokes
final_answer.spoken: any sequence in a fixed order that never runs out and is convenient to count with, for example a circle for every group of five strokes

hold_back: Open answer: any fixed-order sequence that never runs out and is convenient to count with; for example, a circle for every group of five strokes
never_show: the answer card before the last beat of the board solution
maths_rules: a stroke counts 1, a circle counts 5 strokes, a square counts 5 circles, and the rule goes on
never ends: a bigger mark can be made whenever 5 of the last mark are collected
convenient: 13 = 5 + 5 + 3, so 13 objects need 2 circles and 3 strokes, which is 5 marks instead of 13
video_script.design: One idea: a number system is tested by two questions, ending and convenience. The marks stay on the stage; one example is built and tested. Other choices are welcome.

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, we may choose any marks we like, as long as they follow a fixed order.

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find a system that never ends and is convenient to count with.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: choose the marks: a stroke for 1; a circle for 5 strokes; a square for 5 circles; and so on

marks.m1: five strokes gather into a circle, and five circles gather into a square

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>A stroke counts one object. Five strokes make a circle, and five circles make a square.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: does it end? Whenever 5 of the last mark are collected, a bigger mark can be made, so the sequence never ends

marks.m2: five squares gather into a bigger mark, with an arrow marked and so on, and a tick appears on never ends

narration: <bookmark mark='s2'/>Step two, ask if it ever ends.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Whenever five of the last mark are collected, a bigger mark can be made. The sequence never ends.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: is it convenient? 13 = 5 + 5 + 3, so 13 objects need 2 circles and 3 strokes: 5 marks, not 13

marks.m3: thirteen strokes regroup into two circles and three strokes, and a tick appears on convenient

narration: <bookmark mark='s3'/>Step three, ask if it is convenient. Try thirteen objects.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Thirteen is five and five and three. That is two circles and three strokes, so five marks and not thirteen.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check: 2 circles are 5 + 5 = 10, and 10 + 3 strokes = 13

marks.m4: the two circles turn back into ten strokes, the three strokes join them, and the total reads thirteen

narration: <bookmark mark='s4'/>Step four, put the marks back to check.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Two circles are five and five, which is ten. Ten and three strokes make thirteen, so the marks are right.

beats.on_screen: Answer: Open answer: any fixed-order sequence that never runs out and is convenient to count with; for example, a circle for every group of five strokes
narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>A fixed order that never runs out and is convenient makes a number system.
<bookmark mark='res'/>Any such sequence is a good answer. One example is a circle for every group of five strokes.
